title: Eagles QB Jalen Hurts Faces Season-Ending Outlook After Blood Clots in Lungs and Leg
body:
Philadelphia’s star quarterback Jalen Hurts has been diagnosed with blood clots in both his lungs and his left leg, a condition that medical staff say will keep him out for the remainder of the 2026 NFL season. The revelation, confirmed by the Eagles on Monday, ends the Super Bowl MVP’s campaign just weeks after he led the team to a dramatic playoff run and sparked hopes of a championship repeat.

Hurts, 26, first reported feeling shortness of breath and leg swelling during a routine training session on the team’s practice field. Subsequent imaging revealed multiple pulmonary emboli and a deep‑vein thrombosis (DVT) in his left calf. He was immediately placed on anticoagulant therapy and transferred to a specialized cardiac‑vascular unit for monitoring. While doctors are optimistic about a full recovery, they cautioned that the treatment regimen and the risk of re‑occurrence preclude any return to contact sport for the rest of the year.

The timing could not be more consequential for Philadelphia. Hurts had been the centerpiece of an offense that combined a potent rushing attack with an efficient passing game, guiding the Eagles to a 13‑4 record and a berth in the NFC Championship before a late‑season ankle injury sidelined him for the final regular‑season game. His absence now forces the coaching staff to rely on backup quarterbacks—most notably the veteran second‑stringer who has limited starting experience and a rookie drafted in the first round who has yet to see meaningful snaps. The shift will test head coach Nick Sirianni’s play‑calling flexibility and the depth of the offensive line, which has already been battered by injuries.

From a broader league perspective, Hurts’ health scare underscores the growing awareness of vascular complications among elite athletes. While deep‑vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism are more commonly associated with long‑haul travel or prolonged immobility, recent studies suggest that high‑intensity training, dehydration, and even certain performance‑enhancing supplements can elevate clotting risk. The NFL’s health and safety committee has already begun reviewing protocols for early detection, including routine Doppler ultrasounds and blood‑coagulation panels for players with a family history of clotting disorders. Hurts’ case may accelerate those efforts, prompting teams to adopt more aggressive screening measures.

For the Eagles, the immediate priority is to stabilize Hurts’s condition while maintaining competitive momentum. Offensive coordinator Shane Steichen has hinted at a more run‑heavy scheme in the coming weeks, leaning on running backs Kenneth Gainwell and Miles Sanders to shoulder the workload. Defensively, the team’s pass rush, anchored by Haason Reddick and Josh Allen, will need to keep opposing offenses in check to compensate for any offensive shortfall. The organization also faces a delicate balancing act in managing public expectations; fans who have rallied around Hurts’s leadership and charismatic persona will be looking for reassurance that the franchise remains in contention.

Looking ahead, the recovery timeline for blood clots varies widely, but most athletes can resume full activity after a three‑ to six‑month course of anticoagulation, followed by a graduated return‑to‑play protocol. If Hurts follows a typical trajectory, he could be back in training camp for the 2027 season, provided no complications arise. In the meantime, the Eagles will need to navigate the remainder of the schedule without their marquee player, a challenge that could either expose depth deficiencies or galvanize a collective “next man up” mentality. The coming weeks will reveal how the team adapts, and whether Philadelphia can still mount a postseason push without the quarterback who helped lift them to the brink of another Super Bowl.
